642.t: Plasterer's apprentice and hearing John Marrero
642.s: Family trades were plastering and bricklaying; at 16 he apprenticed as a plasterer until hearing John Marrero decided him on the banjo.
642.q: Oh no, no indeed. No indeed, man, no indeed. You see, my father was a plasterer. And my uncle was a bricklayer, and my grandfather was a plasterer. And it was just the customs of the Creoles that nobody was supposed to break away from nothing. If he was a plasterer, then I was supposed to be a…

615.t: Deciding on a music career and parental support
615.s: He decided at about thirteen to be a musician; his parents supported him despite hints about medicine.
615.q: I think I pretty much decided that when I was about thirteen. I was performing all the time and felt comfortable doing it, and figured that I could probably make a living doing it.

655.t: Family support, engineering degree and other careers
655.s: His family urged a degree. He studied engineering, worked at an insurance company and got a real estate license, but always wanted drums.
655.q: They were always supportive and they strongly invited and suggested that at least I get a college degree. Well they were looking out for my best interests I’m sure, just for my own edification. And I’m a fairly sensible person, give or take. So it made sense to me. And I just have sort of an…

497.t: Parents' attitudes to a music career and the Northwestern math scholarship
497.s: His mother opposed music, his father left it to him, and he nearly became a computer programmer after a math scholarship to Northwestern.
497.q: I’ll tell you, my mother, you asked me about my father but I’m going to tell you about my mother and say she would say no. Clearly. She didn’t want me to do that. My father didn’t say yes or no. He decided if it was in me, that’s the way it would be. So I never

326.t: Whether music was a deliberate career choice
326.s: Green says he fell into music because his older brothers led the way and the trombone was there.
326.q: I suppose so. I think you were talking to Houston Person earlier about if you just fall into it or what. I think I actually just kind of fell into it because the older brothers kind of led the way, you know, and the trombone was there, and you might as well play it, it’s there, you know. And let’s…

442.t: Supportive parents and studying at Manhattan School and Juilliard
442.s: His Puerto Rican mother loved music; his father urged an education.
442.q: Yeah, yeah they were. My dad and my mom — she’s Puerto Rican. She used to sing in Puerto Rico as a young girl and actually she loved music. And my dad, see my dad was a businessman and he said, “Look, okay. You want to be a musician that’s great. But get an education.” And I said, “Okay. That…

353.t: Father's attitude to her music career and choosing to teach
353.s: After a technical aside, she says her father was unhappy about a music career; she planned to teach music, then switched.
353.ch: Aunt Alma Hightower and Alton Redd
353.q: He wasn’t too happy about it. Because I really didn’t start off to have a career in music. You just were going to play something. You’re going to do music. And then by the time I got out of high school I wanted to teach music. And my first two years in college that’s what I started out to be, a…

110.t: Switching to music; father's offer of partnership on the ranch
110.s: A zoology professor sends him to the conservatory; his father says he can always come back to the ranch, and the Birdland owner later laughs at that line.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: It’s really up to my zoology teacher. Dr. Arnold said to me, “Brubeck, why don’t you go across the lawn to the conservatory, because your mind is not here in the lab.” I took his advice. Went across the lawn to the conservatory the next year.

370.s: She wanted to go to art school but her mother and family did not encourage her; she pursued men instead.
370.ch: Alfred Lion and early Blue Note

80.t: Why he left Alabama; his father's warning to be damn good
80.s: With nothing in Evergreen, he wanted to play his horn and further his education; he recalls deciding on music at four and his father telling him he had to be damned good.
80.q: Well, I had to -- well, not exactly. Yes, I could say yes and no. I had to have some place to live, and I never being east, or north, or I'd never been out of Evergreen, only just a couple little places around there, you know? So I felt I had something to offer, and I wanted to get out where I…

230.t: Deciding to be a musician and his family's attitude
230.s: He always wanted to be a musician; family neither encouraged nor opposed it, though they might have preferred a lawyer.
230.q: Yeah, back to the hatbox days. And while I wasn't encouraged about it, I wasn't stomped on about it. I mean, nobody said, "Don't you dare touch that horn again," or anything like that. And then I didn't, like, go against the complete wishes of my family, as some people would

452.t: Back from the hospital: Larkin's uniform and his mother's objection
452.s: After the hospital Cobb rehearses with Milton Larkin, who brings his uniform; his mother protests but her sister persuades her to let him go.
452.q: All right, I came back -- I was sick. I went in the hospital; I had plurisy, and Milt Larkin, after I come out of the hospital -- I was at Jefferson Davis, and I was doing mighty fine; I was waiting on people in the hospital, and walking around because I was young -- too young to die.

120.t: Choosing music over radio, and parents warning girls off a musician
120.s: As a boy he hesitates between electrician and music; people say musicians amount to nothing and the girls' mothers tell them to avoid him.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: You know, in looking back on my life in the music business, it certainly had some pitfalls here and there; I can remember the early days when I toring between whether I should get into radio - I had a radio set - I was toring between whether I wanted to be an electrician of some kind - you know -…

233.t: The thought of becoming a musician
233.s: Monk wondered whether he could be a musician but knew it was not simple, and felt nothing he had achieved matched expression.
233.q: Oh, no. Because I knew even those times when the height of my thing was when I bought the car, the height of that was nothing in comparison to what he had gone through. You see, I was busy doing what I thought was the greatest thing, to work this job and to achieve so-and-so. But none of that meant…

418.t: Training to be a contractor and the ladder accident that led to music
418.s: His father wanted him to be a plastering contractor; a broken ladder rung sprained his back and he turned to playing.
418.q: Well, I was going to be a (?) contractor. That's what my father wanted me to be. So he had to start from the bottom. And from the bottom meant that you had to mix the sand and the mortar and stuff together. Then you had to carry it. And in those days they had laddering(?), like foot(?) ladder(?)…
